newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Britain denies change of tack on EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Britain denies change of tack on EMU.

text.p: British finance minister Kenneth Clarke on Wednesday denied that remarks on the single currency by Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind signalled a change in government policy.
"The foreign secretary wasn't intending to change the position of the government," Clarke told reporters.
Rifkind, speaking earlier on BBC radio, said the government was hostile to the single currency planned for launch in 1999.
"On balance we are hostile to a single currency, but we accept you have to think very carefully about these matters before you rule them out completely," he said.

Clarke said Rifkind's comments appeared to be a slip of the tongue under pressure from a skilful interviewer and the foreign secretary said later that his remarks were "based on our well-established position".
However, Conservative Eurosceptics opposed to closer European ties were jubilant at what they saw as a clear shift in position by Rifkind.

Senior Conservatives said the foreign secretary was expressing government policy agreed by the cabinet on January 23, when ministers argued for a delay in EMU on the grounds it was very unlikely the single currency could be launched safely.

Major has told parliament it was unlikely, though not impossible, that the single currency could proceed safely on January 1, 1999. If it did proceed without reliable convergence, Britain would not be part of it, he added.
"We've already said it would be dangerous to proceed and it was on that basis that the foreign secretary was speaking," a government official said.
Major said on Wednesday supporters of a single European currency would have to show it was "positively beneficial" before Britain should consider signing up.
